projects.title: Personal Portfolio
projects.outcome: Fast, installable, and playful - the site you're on right now, with a hidden shell for the curious.

caseStudy.tagline: One content source, three interfaces — including a real shell with a virtual filesystem.
highlights: Normal, fun and terminal modes rendered from a single content source
24 shell commands over a virtual filesystem built from that same content
Installable PWA with caching tuned so the 3D bundle stays lazy

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
A portfolio has to serve two audiences that want opposite things. Recruiters want the facts quickly. Engineers want to poke at something.

So this site offers three ways in — a direct normal mode, a motion-designed fun mode, and a terminal mode that is an actual shell — all rendered from one content source, so nothing can drift out of sync.

sections.heading: One source, four surfaces
sections.body:
Everything lives in a single content tree. All three modes read it, and so does the CV, which is generated client-side with jsPDF rather than being a separate uploaded file.

That last part matters more than it sounds: a portfolio whose downloadable résumé disagrees with the page it sits on is a very common and very avoidable failure. Here the two cannot disagree, because there is only one set of facts.

At runtime the app boots from a baked-in copy of that tree — instant first paint, works offline — then fetches the live version from Supabase and swaps it in. If Supabase is unreachable the bundled copy simply stays.

sections.heading: The terminal
sections.body:
Not a gimmick with three canned responses. Twenty-four commands over a virtual filesystem built from the site's own content.

Navigation and reading are real: ls, cd, cat, head, tree, pwd, and a grep that searches file contents rather than names. The shell furniture is there too — help, per-command man pages, history, clear, echo, whoami, neofetch and a joke sudo. Two commands, fx and scene, drive the live 3D backdrop from the prompt.

The filesystem models two kinds of node. Text files render inline through cat; binary files carry a href and a size and are handled by open — so cat on a PDF does something sensible instead of dumping bytes at you.
bullets: Paths are normalised strings, so navigation behaves the way a shell user expects
The tree rebuilds from the latest content before each render, so CMS edits appear without a redeploy
Output is word-wrapped to the terminal frame — the kind of thing you only add after watching it look wrong
A sentinel line inside a text file is swapped by the renderer for a real contact button, so text output can contain an interactive element without the filesystem knowing anything about React

sections.heading: The chunk that got faster by being ignored
sections.body:
The instinct with a large 3D dependency is to force it into its own vendor chunk. Doing that here made things measurably worse.

Naming three.js, React Three Fiber and easy-3dkit as a manual chunk pulled them into the entry graph, so roughly a megabyte was statically imported and executed on the landing page. Left to the bundler's default behaviour, they stay inside the lazily-loaded terminal chunk and are fetched only when someone actually opens the terminal.

Only two chunks are named — the React runtime, which loads on every page anyway, and the animation library, which is dynamically imported by the mode pages. Both are named for long-term caching, not for size.

The reasoning is written into the config, so the optimisation cannot be helpfully undone by a future edit.

sections.heading: A service worker that respects lazy loading
sections.body:
The same decision had to be made twice. The service worker precaches the app shell — styles, markup, icons, fonts and normal-sized scripts — but explicitly excludes the heavy 3D bundle, which is runtime-cached on first use instead.

Precaching it would have eagerly downloaded roughly 900 kilobytes at install time and quietly undone the lazy loading the bundler config worked to preserve. Deep links fall back to the app shell so navigation works offline, and the worker auto-updates with claim-and-skip-waiting so a deploy never serves stale content.

sections.heading: The CMS nobody expects
sections.body:
The site is not static. Behind it sits Supabase: three migrations covering an admin CMS schema, contact replies and outbound message composition, plus three edge functions for notifying on a new contact submission and sending replies.

An authenticated admin area edits every part of the content tree through structured forms — no raw JSON — with publish-time validation, a per-save history snapshot for undo, and media upload for case-study screenshots and demo clips.

The seed script that pushes content into the database carries a security note next to the code that needs it: it runs with the service-role key, which bypasses row-level security, so it must never be committed or shipped. Knowing that, and writing it where the next person will read it, is what prevents the most common way these projects leak.

sections.heading: Dogfooding
sections.body:
The live 3D backdrop runs on easy-3dkit — my own npm package — as a real dependency rather than vendored source.

That closes a loop in both directions. The site gets its visuals from the library; the library gets a consumer that exercises its published artifact, which is how packaging regressions surface before a stranger finds them.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: Fast, installable and playful — the site you are on right now, with a hidden shell for the curious, a content pipeline that keeps every surface saying the same thing, and performance decisions documented where they were made rather than in a changelog nobody reads.

projects.description: Designer and builder of my personal portfolio - a React/Vite site with Framer Motion motion design, a live Three.js/R3F backdrop powered by my own easy-3dkit, and an installable PWA. Ships a fully interactive terminal mode with a virtual filesystem and command parser as an alternate way to explore the site.

research.title: Cascaded AI Task Decomposition (CATD)
research.status: Accepted subject to minor revision — NCCS, June 2026
research.summary: A generalizable design pattern for multi-stage computer vision pipelines, validated on bi-scriptual Nepali license-plate recognition.
research.citation: Sigdel, A., Thapa, S., Thapa Magar, B., & Gajurel, R.K. "Cascaded AI Task Decomposition: A Generalizable Framework for Multi-Stage Computer Vision Pipelines Validated on Automated Number Plate Recognition for Nepali License Plates."
highlights: Formalized the CATD framework as a generalizable design pattern for multi-stage CV pipelines with applications beyond ANPR.
Achieved 97.1% mAP@50 plate localization and 97.8% mAP@50 character recognition on the held-out test set, using custom-trained YOLOv11n and RF-DETR Base across 61 bi-scriptual Nepali plate classes.

Built a two-dimensional cross-domain training strategy (1,380 Nepali flat + 1,127 Indian embossed plates) enabling compositional zero-shot transfer to embossed plates absent from training (+24.5 pp under specular reflection).
Engineered a three-stage cascaded pipeline (YOLOv8n → YOLOv11n → RF-DETR Base) with an estimated 90.4% end-to-end precision and 61%–73% compute reduction via intelligent vehicle gating.
Integrated the system as the computer-vision backbone of a smart-parking platform handling automated billing and real-time traffic analytics.
